sources.use: Supports beginner puck pursuit, getting available for a pass, broad skill development and respectful conduct. US age categories do not establish Canadian game rules.

replacement.limits: Static experimental illustration. Coaching responses and reference positions are suggestions. No skating, tactical mastery or learning transfer is certified. An adult may read questions and record spoken reflections.

questions.prompt: Who starts with the puck?
questions.explanation: The puck is attached to Navy2.

questions.prompt: What is YOUR job in this activity?

options.text: Skate over and take the puck from Navy2
Wait with your back to Navy2

questions.explanation: The briefing identifies YOU as the receiver. Taking the puck from your partner, or turning away from them, would end the partner pass before it starts.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple partner pass.

options.text: Get ready for the gentle pass

questions.explanation: This is a suggested progression. The eventual pass needs its own explicit movement; it is not shown yet.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer, leaving space between partners.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance. Other clear receiving places could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 is not ready yet. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can wait or communicate instead of forcing the activity.

questions.prompt: How could you show your partner you are ready?
questions.explanation: A clear look or simple call can help. Discuss a receiving target with the coach; no physical technique is graded.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2’s pass slides a little behind YOU. What could YOU do?

options.text: Turn and skate to the puck under control
Wait for Navy2 to come and get it
Reach across without moving your feet

questions.explanation: Missing the first touch is normal in practice. Turning and going to the puck keeps the activity going. Reaching without moving your feet often puts you off balance, and waiting leaves the puck where it stopped. Nothing in this picture shows how hard or how fast a pass would be.

questions.prompt: Which two things can YOU see that help YOU get ready?

options.text: The ice between YOU and Navy2 is open

questions.explanation: The picture shows the puck with Navy2 and no player standing between the partners. It does not show sticks or which hand anyone shoots with, so that is not a cue YOU can read here.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a second waiting spot that keeps the ice to Navy2 open.
questions.explanation: No player stands between this spot and Navy2, and Navy2 would not have to turn far to see YOU. Gold1 is not part of this try, so the choice is about staying visible to your partner. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the ice between the partners stays clear.

questions.prompt: Gold1 is not in this try. What would change if Gold1 joined in?
questions.explanation: With nobody challenging, YOU can pick a waiting spot mainly for a clear view of Navy2. If someone joined in, YOU would also check where they are and whether the ice between the partners is still open. This picture does not show that change, so any answer about it is a discussion, not something the scene proves.

sourceChecks.ageFormat: Timbits U7; the page states "Hockey for 5- and 6-year olds" and places U7 at the LTPD "Fundamentals 1" stage.
sourceChecks.claim: U7 is 5- and 6-year-olds at LTPD Fundamentals 1. "Only 15% of practice time should be spent on individual tactics, with 85% of practice time spent on skills." The U7 skills matrix lists Balance and Agility, Edge Control (inside edge glide, figure 8s, slalom), Starting and Stopping (including two-foot parallel stop and outside leg stop), Forward and Backward Skating, Turning and Crossovers, Stationary and Moving Puck Control (including "Open ice carry - forehand & backhand"), Stationary and Moving Passing and Receiving, Shooting, Individual Offensive Tactics (body fakes, stick fakes) and Individual Defensive Tactics (angling).
sourceChecks.scope: Fetched and read as HTML on 2026-09-05; HTTP 200. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE PACKET-01 RETURN: this URL was recorded there as "unavailable, HTTP 403". It is not blocked. It returns 200 to plain curl when a normal browser User-Agent is sent, so the earlier 403 was a fetch-tool artefact rather than the site's behaviour. Supports age placement, the vocabulary in these scenes (edges, stopping, open-ice carry, passing and receiving) and the 15/85 tactics-to-skills split that argues against systems content at U7. It certifies no answer key, no coordinate and no learning transfer.

sourceChecks.claim: U7 games are cross-ice for the entire season on a surface of at most 100 ft by 60 ft, 4-on-4 plus a player defending the goal, two periods on a run-time clock, shifts of at most two minutes, no icing and no offside, "No score is kept, and game sheets are optional", "Incidental contact may happen, but body-checking is not permitted", a three-metre back-off on a change of possession, and "Blue puck (4 oz) is preferred".
sourceChecks.scope: Fetched and read as HTML on 2026-09-05; HTTP 200 (again, not the 403 recorded in packet-01). Supports two specific things in this packet: that a full-rink drawing is an orientation aid rather than the U7 match layout, which these scenes already declare in their own briefings and limits; and that the blue puck is a real U7 detail, which is why "Only if it is blue" is a confusing distractor rather than a harmlessly silly one. It also confirms no score is kept at U7, which makes exp26-u7-005-q1's "Change the score" wrong for a sourced reason. It certifies no coordinate, no answer key and no claim about any of these scenes' teaching value.

"Developing strong scanning habits is essential - constantly reading the play, assessing the positions of defenders and identifying open areas of the ice." Puck control creates time and space by forcing defenders to react.

sourceChecks.ageFormat: 8-and-Under, printed pp.6-8 = PDF pp.12-14. US 8U spans roughly ages 7-8, so it is NOT the same band as Hockey Canada U7 (5-6). The catalog page references are accurate.
sourceChecks.claim: Player Knowledge lists Puck Pursuit and Puck Support: "Players should learn to make themselves available to receive a pass from a teammate. This is the beginning of the idea of 'getting open.'" Team Concepts adds "near- and far-support concepts, as well as creating and finding passing lanes". Individual skills include "receiving a pass properly with the stick"; Body Contact at this level is "stick on puck" and "stick lift". The manual states 8U players "are not at a cognitive level where they should be lectured on" these topics, and that "no time be spent on teaching systems related to team-play in 8-and-Under hockey".
sourceChecks.scope: Downloaded (1.26 MB, 68 pages) and read with pypdf on 2026-09-05. Supports the receiving and getting-open objective of exp26-u7-006 and the passing-lane vocabulary in exp26-u7-003 q7, which is why I did not flag that vocabulary as out of band. It also supports the scenes' adult-co-reading limits and argues against systems content at this age. It certifies no answer key, no geometry and no Canadian rule; the age-band difference is a real limit on how far it can be carried across to a Hockey Canada U7 scene.
